chapters.title: Chapter 5: Evaluating Startups and Building Your Portfolio

lessons.title: Red Flags and Common Mistakes First-Time Angels Make

children.text: Most startups you back will fail, and much of that is outside your control. But a surprising share of angel losses are avoidable. They come from warning signs that were visible before the money moved, or from the investor's own behaviour: rushing, following famous names, doubling down on a sinking company. This lesson pulls together the red flags that should stop or slow a deal, walks through one of India's most visible governance collapses, and lists the behavioural mistakes first-time angels make most often, with a fix for each.

body.text: You cannot avoid startup failure, but you can avoid unforced errors. The two biggest sources of preventable losses are ignoring red flags in the deal and letting emotions make your decisions.

markDefs.definition: A transaction between the company and a person or business connected to its founders or directors, such as the startup buying services from a founder's other company.
A large shareholding held by someone no longer working in the company, such as a departed co-founder, which can make future fundraising harder.

children.text: No single red flag proves a startup is bad. But each one should make you slow down and ask harder questions, and some, like refusing to share documents, should end the conversation. Two terms come up often: a

body.caption: Deal red flags and why they matter

cells: Process
"The round closes on Friday, decide now"
Artificial urgency is designed to stop you doing diligence
Process
Money requested before agreements are shared
Once you have paid, you have lost all negotiating leverage
Numbers
Refuses to share bank statements, GST returns or audited accounts
Genuine founders with real numbers rarely hide them from serious investors
Numbers
Pitch metrics do not match MCA filings or GST data
Either the pitch is inflated or the filings are wrong; both are serious
Numbers
MCA annual filings overdue or audited accounts long delayed
Delayed accounts are often the first public sign of deeper problems
Governance
Significant related-party transactions
Company money can flow to founders' other businesses
Governance
Messy cap table or dead equity
Future investors may refuse to invest until it is cleaned up
Founders
Large founder salaries or founders selling shares in a seed round
Your money should build the company, not cash out the founders
Terms
Participating preferences or full ratchet for other investors at seed
Your payout is heavily reduced in most realistic outcomes
Pitch
Guaranteed returns, buyback promises or celebrity names as the main proof
Real startup risk cannot be guaranteed; famous names are not diligence

children.text: Case Study: The Warning Lights at Byju's

Byju's was once India's most valuable startup, reported at a valuation of $22 billion, backed by some of the world's best-known investors. Its troubles became public through exactly the kind of governance signals in the table above.

body.title: Governance warning signs at Byju's, as publicly reported

events.title: Delayed accounts
events.description: Audited financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2022 remain long delayed.

events.title: Regulatory searches
events.description: The Enforcement Directorate searches Byju's premises over suspected violations of foreign exchange laws.

events.title: Auditor resigns
events.description: Deloitte resigns as statutory auditor, citing the long delay in the FY22 financial statements.

events.title: Board exits reported
events.description: Board members representing Sequoia Capital, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and Prosus reportedly resign. Byju's calls the auditor change a planned transition and disputes the reported board exits.

events.title: Second auditor exits
events.description: BDO, which replaced Deloitte, also resigns as auditor, according to media reports.

body.text: Delayed audited accounts, an auditor resigning and investor directors leaving the board are among the clearest governance alarms there are. The same signals apply to a ₹5 crore seed-stage company: ask for audited accounts, check whether its annual filings on the MCA portal are up to date, and ask why if an auditor or a director has recently left.

children.text: Mistakes Angels Make: The Enemy in the Mirror

markDefs.definition: The tendency to assume something is a good decision because other people, especially famous or successful ones, have made it.
Continuing to put money into something because of what you have already spent, rather than because of its future prospects.

children.text: Even with a perfect checklist, angels make predictable behavioural mistakes. The two most expensive are
, backing a deal because someone impressive already did, and the
, adding money to rescue an earlier cheque.

body.caption: Ten common angel mistakes and their fixes

cells: FOMO
Committing within hours because "the round is almost full"
Set a personal cooling-off period before any commitment
Social proof
"A famous founder invested, so it must be good"
Do your own diligence; ask what that investor actually checked
The friendship discount
Skipping diligence because the founder is a friend or relative
Apply the same checklist; it protects the friendship too
Overconfidence after a win
Doubling cheque sizes after one good exit
Stick to the budget and portfolio plan you set in advance
Sunk cost follow-ons
Funding every bridge round to protect the first cheque
Treat each follow-on as a new investment decision
Concentration
Half the angel budget in one or two companies
Size cheques from the plan: budget × (1 − reserves) ÷ companies
Valuation blindness
Ignoring price because "if it works, it will not matter"
Model your return at the entry price; price always matters
Ignoring terms
Reading the valuation, not the preferences and anti-dilution
Read the term sheet clauses from Chapter 4 before committing
Weak records
No folder of agreements, allotment proof or payment records
Keep a document file for every investment from day one
Tax and compliance neglect
Late tax returns, losses not carried forward, foreign investments not disclosed
Work with a chartered accountant and file on time every year

children.text: Valuation blindness deserves its own maths, because hot markets make it tempting. Your eventual proceeds depend directly on the price you paid:

body.latex: \text{Exit proceeds} = \frac{\text{Investment}}{\text{Entry post-money valuation}} \times (1 - \text{Total later dilution}) \times \text{Exit value}
body.caption: Halve the entry valuation and, with everything else equal, you double what you receive at exit.

body.title: The cost of paying up
body.prompt: You invest ₹10 lakh in a startup. In a hot market, you pay a ₹40 crore post-money valuation; a more disciplined angel waited and invested the same ₹10 lakh at ₹20 crore post-money in an earlier close. Later rounds dilute both stakes by a total of 40%, and the company exits at ₹400 crore. How much less do you receive than the disciplined angel, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: You: ₹10 lakh ÷ ₹40 crore = 0.25%, diluted to 0.15%, worth ₹60 lakh at ₹400 crore. Disciplined angel: ₹10 lakh ÷ ₹20 crore = 0.5%, diluted to 0.3%, worth ₹1.2 crore. You receive ₹60 lakh less, 6x instead of 12x, for the same company and the same outcome.

body.label: A simple personal rule
body.value: Never commit on the day you first hear the pitch
body.context: A cooling-off period, even 48 hours, breaks the spell of urgency and gives you time to check documents and speak to people the founder did not introduce. A legitimate round rarely disappears in two days.

body.title: Before you transfer a single rupee
steps: I have waited at least 48 hours since first hearing the pitch.
I have seen bank statements, GST returns and the latest accounts, and they match the pitch.
I have checked the company's MCA filings and cap table.
I have spoken to at least one customer and one former colleague of the founders whom they did not introduce.
I have read the full term sheet, including preference, anti-dilution and pro-rata clauses.
I know exactly who will be the shareholder: me, a registered fund, or an SPV.
The money is going to the company's bank account, not a person.
The cheque fits my angel budget and portfolio plan.
I can afford to lose all of it.

body.text: Be especially wary when a deal combines several red flags with several behavioural triggers: urgency, a friend as founder, a famous name on the cap table and a request to pay before documents arrive. Each one alone is manageable. Together, they are exactly the conditions in which experienced people make their worst decisions.

body.title: Name the bias
body.question: Sunil invests ₹5 lakh in a food-tech startup mainly because a well-known cricketer is already an investor. He does not ask for any financial documents. Which behavioural mistake is this?
body.explanation: Sunil is relying on someone else's decision instead of evidence, which is social proof. A celebrity investor may have invested for publicity, a small amount or on different terms, and is unlikely to have done diligence on Sunil's behalf.

body.title: Aarav's second deal
body.scenario: Aarav, a first-time angel in Kolkata, recently sold his stake in his first startup investment to a later investor for 8x his ₹3 lakh cheque. Energised, he is now considering ₹15 lakh in a gaming startup founded by his college senior. The founder says the round closes in three days, that two film celebrities have already committed, and that GST returns are "not relevant because we are pre-revenue on paper". The shareholders' agreement will be shared "after the money comes in".
body.prompt: List every red flag and behavioural trap in this situation, and say what Aarav should do.
body.modelAnswer:
Behavioural traps:
1. Overconfidence after a win: one 8x exit on a small cheque does not make him a proven stock-picker, yet he wants to write a cheque five times larger.
2. The friendship discount: backing a college senior makes it tempting to skip diligence.
3. Social proof: the celebrity names are being used in place of evidence.
4. FOMO: the three-day deadline is designed to rush him.

Deal red flags:
5. No financial documents, with an excuse for not sharing GST data.
6. Money requested before the shareholders' agreement is shared.

What Aarav should do:
7. Refuse to pay anything before seeing signed agreements, a PAS-4 offer letter and the cap table, and confirm the money goes to the company's account.
8. Ask for bank statements and whatever accounts exist, check MCA filings, and speak to people the founder did not introduce.
9. Recheck the size against his budget: ₹15 lakh may be far above his planned cheque.
10. If the founder will not wait or share documents, walk away. Losing a deal is cheaper than losing ₹15 lakh, and the friendship will survive a polite no better than a failed investment.

body.title: Name the fallacy
body.textWithBlank: Putting more money into a struggling startup mainly to protect an earlier investment is an example of the sunk ___ fallacy.
body.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy makes people keep spending because of money already spent. The only question for a follow-on is whether it is a good investment on its own merits today.

cards.definition: Fear of missing out: committing quickly because others are, or because a deadline seems close.
Assuming a deal is good because famous or successful people have invested.
Adding money to protect past investments rather than because of future prospects.
Overestimating your skill after early wins, often leading to larger, riskier cheques.
A deal between the company and a business or person connected to its founders or directors.
A large stake held by someone no longer working in the company.
A serious governance warning sign, especially when linked to delayed or disputed accounts.
A personal rule never to commit on the same day you first hear a pitch.

points: Treat urgency, refusal to share documents, mismatched numbers and requests to pay before agreements as reasons to slow down or walk away.
Delayed audited accounts, auditor resignations and investor directors leaving are major governance alarms, as the public warning signs at Byju's showed.
Famous investors, friendships and recent wins are the conditions under which angels most often skip diligence.
Price matters: paying twice the valuation halves your exit proceeds for the same outcome.
Treat every follow-on as a fresh decision, and keep cheques within your planned budget and portfolio size.
Use a cooling-off period and a pre-investment checklist, keep full records, and stay on top of tax and compliance.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Information about Byju's is based on public media reports; the company disputed some reported events, and related matters may be contested or ongoing. Sunil, Aarav and all illustrative figures are hypothetical. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
